title: "Dense Layer"
description: "A neural-network layer in which each input unit connects to each output unit."
term: "Dense Layer"
letter: "D"

difficulty: "Beginner"

## Simple explanation

A dense layer, also called a fully connected layer, combines all its input
values to calculate each output value. It is a common building block in
neural networks.

## Technical explanation

For input vector $x$, weights $W$, and bias $b$, a dense layer computes
$y = Wx+b$, often followed by an activation function. Each output unit
has a learned weight for every input unit, so parameter count grows with
both input and output dimensions.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Dense layers can combine features into task-specific predictions, such
as class scores. Their parameter and compute costs can become large for
high-dimensional inputs, which motivates other structures such as
convolutions or low-rank projections.

## How it works

The layer multiplies the input by a learned weight matrix, adds a learned
bias vector, and optionally applies a nonlinearity. During training,
backpropagation computes gradients for the weights and biases.

## Practical example

After an image model extracts a feature vector, a dense output layer can
map that vector to two class scores for penguin and ostrich.

## Common misconceptions

- A dense layer does not necessarily mean every neuron in the whole model
  is connected to every other neuron.
- The layer's linear transformation alone cannot represent arbitrary
  nonlinear relationships without nonlinearities elsewhere.
- A larger dense layer is not automatically more capable in a useful way.
